abstract.p: The long-eared hedgehog, Hemiechinus auritus, has the broadest distribution among Erinaceidae, yet its intraspecific taxonomy remains contentious, with three to six subspecies recognized. We examined the phylogeographic structure of the species across nearly its entire distribution range using two mitochondrial genes (cytb, COI) for 153 specimens from 103 localities, complemented by complete mitogenomes for seven individuals. Phylogenetic reconstructions recovered five deeply divergent, well-supported mitochondrial lineages (p-distances 2–4%): Northern, Eastern, Transcaucasian, South-western and Southern. The Southern lineage, which includes specimens from the type locality of H. a. megalotis, was recovered as the basal branch, whereas the Northern and Eastern lineages formed a derived clade. Demographic analyses indicated recent postglacial expansion in the Northern and Eastern lineages, but not in the Southern and South-western lineages. Species distribution modelling reconstructed Pleistocene range fragmentation during glacial maxima, with divergence among lineages dated to the late Middle and Late Pleistocene. The mitochondrial lineages are partly congruent with the main morphological subspecies, although the status of H. a. megalotis and H. collaris requires further scrutiny. Our results indicate that H. auritus may represent a complex of several divergent lineages, whose evolutionary independence and taxonomic status should be tested with nuclear genomic data.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Compared to rodents, the order Eulipotyphla contains significantly fewer species adapted to open, arid landscapes. Among the most well-known of these are the spiny hedgehogs of the genera Paraechinus, Hemiechinus, and Mesechinus. The evolutionary history of these genera is inextricably linked to the development of arid biomes across the Palearctic. Originating in the Late Miocene [1], they have evolved through the colonization of steppe and desert habitats. Consequently, studying the range dynamics of these groups provides valuable insights into the biogeographic and paleoclimatic history of the landscapes they inhabit.

The long-eared hedgehog Hemiechinus auritus (Gmelin, 1770) occupies vast areas of the western Palearctic and has the broadest distribution of any species within both the subfamily Erinaceinae and the family Erinaceidae as a whole. Its range extends across north-eastern Africa, the Middle East (including Asia Minor and Cyprus), south-eastern Europe, Iran, Afghanistan, and most of Central Asia northward to western Siberia and eastward to Mongolia, reaching as far east as northern China [2,3]. Ecologically, it is widespread across steppe and desert landscapes, and frequently occupies anthropogenic environments such as gardens and urban parks [4]. The genus Hemiechinus contains one additional species, the Indian long-eared hedgehog H. collaris Gray, 1830 [3,5,6], which, in stark contrast, is restricted to a much smaller range in Pakistan and north-western and north-central India.

The long-eared hedgehog exhibits substantial intraspecific morphological variation, which has resulted in a rather unstable and debated subspecific taxonomy. Different authors recognize anywhere from three to six subspecies [2,3,6,7]. This taxonomic ambiguity is most pronounced regarding the southern form, currently recognized as the subspecies H. a. megalotis. It was originally described as a distinct species, H. megalotis Blyth, 1845; however, many researchers have since downgraded it to a subspecies [8,9], whereas others have advocated its full species status [10].

Given the complex patterns of intraspecific morphological variability and the historically debated subspecific taxonomy across its vast range, H. auritus is hypothesized to exhibit significant genetic structuring. While previous genetic studies have been restricted to specific geographic regions—such as Iran [9,11], the Anatolian Peninsula, northern Cyprus, and Azerbaijan [12], as well as Central Asia, south-eastern Europe, and Africa [1]—they consistently demonstrate considerable phylogeographic structure within the species.

In the present study, we examine the phylogeographic structure of the long-eared hedgehog across nearly its entire range. We use a large dataset comprising two mitochondrial gene fragments, complemented by complete mitogenomes for a subset of samples. Furthermore, we estimate the timing of divergence among the major geographical lineages and perform biogeographic reconstructions to elucidate the evolutionary history of H. auritus. Recognizing that geographically defined mitochondrial haplogroups are not necessarily equivalent to morphological subspecies or valid species, we nevertheless compare the distribution of these haplogroups with the ranges of known subspecies to evaluate the relationship between genetic and morphological variation.

sec.title: 2.1. Molecular Procedures
sec.p: The whole dataset for Hemiechinus auritus comprises 153 specimens from 104 localities across the species’ distribution in Eurasia and Africa (Figure 1, Supplementary Materials SI Table S1-A). Among them, 38 sequences of the cytochrome b gene (cytb), 5 sequences of the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I (COI) gene, and two complete mitochondrial genomes were retrieved from GenBank. We also analyzed cytb, COI, and complete mitochondrial genome sequences of the following taxa used as outgroups: Paraechinus aethiopicus, P. hypomelas, P. micropus, P. nudiventris, Mesechinus dauuricus, M. hughi, M. miodon, M. wangi, and M. orientalis. For the phylogenetic analysis of the mitogenomes, additional outgroups were included: Atelerix albiventris, Erinaceus europaeus, E. concolor, and E. amurensis (Table S1-B).

The material primarily consisted of tissue samples preserved in 96% ethanol, housed in the tissue collection of the Zoological Museum and the Department of Vertebrate Zoology at Moscow State University (ZMMU). Additionally, 11 specimens of H. auritus and one historical specimen of H. collaris were represented by archival DNA extracted from museum skins (age of historical specimens ranging from 50 to 135 years).

Genomic DNA was isolated from ethanol-fixed tissues following the conventional procedure of proteinase K digestion, purification with phenol–chloroform, and precipitation with isopropanol [13]. For museum specimens, DNA was isolated from fragments of dried skin with the DNeasy Blood & Tissue and QIAamp DNA Investigator kits (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions and the guidelines of Yang et al. [14] with several modifications: samples were lysed overnight at 56 °C; the elution buffer was pre-warmed to 56 °C, and after it had been applied, the column was left at room temperature for 7–10 min and then centrifuged for 1 min at 14,000 rpm (Eppendorf Minispin benchtop centrifuge; Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany).

We sequenced the complete cytochrome b gene (cytb) for 97 recent specimens and fragments (180–600 bp) for 12 historical museum specimens. A 687 bp fragment of COI was sequenced for 49 specimens. In addition, nearly complete mitochondrial genomes were obtained for 7 specimens of H. auritus.

The entire cytb gene (1140 bp) was amplified with primers L-hemi_glu/H-hemi_pro from Bannikova et al. [1] according to the corresponding PCR protocols, and sequenced using primers H625 and L535 designed specifically for this study (Table S2). Amplification conditions consisted of an initial denaturation at 94 °C for 3 min, followed by 35 cycles of 94 °C for 1 min, 57 °C for 1 min, and 72 °C for 1 min, with a final extension at 72 °C for 6 min.

A fragment of the COI gene was amplified and sequenced in a single PCR using primers L11b/H742 (Table S2). Reaction conditions were identical to those for cytb, except that the extension step was shortened to 30 s. PCR products were visualized on 1% agarose gels and purified using the Diatom DNA Clean-Up kit (Isogen, Moscow, Russia).

Purified amplicons (10–40 ng) of cytb and COI were sequenced in both directions using Sanger sequencing on an ABI 3100-Avant automated sequencer using ABI PRISM® BigDye™ Terminator v3.1 chemistry (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA, USA). To obtain complete mitogenomes, total DNA libraries were sequenced using SURFSeq (GeneMind Biosciences, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China) and NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) platforms with paired-end read lengths of 150 bp and 100 bp, respectively.

Because DNA from museum specimens was strongly degraded, short overlapping fragments were amplified for most historical samples, as well as for degraded tissues of road-killed animals, using various combinations of the internal primers mentioned above together with additional primers developed for this study (Table S2). Short fragments were amplified under the following cycling conditions: 95 °C for 3 min; 45 cycles of 30 s at 95 °C, 30 s at 51–58 °C (the annealing temperature depended on the primer pair, Table S3), and 30 s at 72 °C; and a final step of 6 min at 72 °C. A negative control was processed in parallel at every stage of DNA extraction. To prevent contamination, all extractions and amplifications of DNA from museum material were performed in the ZMMU Laboratory of Historical DNA, a facility used exclusively for museum samples and never for work with fresh tissues. Aliquots of the extracts (10 µL) were checked by electrophoresis in a 1% agarose gel against a 100 bp ladder.

The newly obtained sequences are available in GenBank under accession numbers: cytb QB057467–QB057575; COI QB047202–QB047250; mitogenomes QB082343–QB082345, QB133264, QB133265, QB144923, QB147350 (Tables S1-A and S1-B).

sec.title: 2.2. Phylogenetic Analysis
sec.p: All sequences were aligned using ClustalW in BioEdit 7.0.9.0 [15]. The final cytb alignment included 1140 bp for 139 sequences of H. auritus, one sequence of H. collaris and 7 outgroups. The concatenated alignment of cytb and COI (1827 bp in total, including 687 bp of COI) included 49 specimens of H. auritus and two outgroups (Mesechinus dauuricus and M. miodon). Of these, both markers were available for 47 specimens of H. auritus and for both outgroups. Two specimens from Afghanistan (USNM:MAMM:602259 and USNM:MAMM:602256) were represented by COI sequences from GenBank only. In the phylogenetic analysis of mitogenomes, we used a concatenated alignment of 12 protein-coding genes (PCGs) (10809 bp, ND6 excluded).

Maximum likelihood (ML) trees were reconstructed using IQTree version 1.6 [16]. The ModelFinder routine [17] was applied to select the optimum partitioning schemes and substitution models for each data subset according to the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). For single-gene analyses, the cytb dataset was partitioned by three codon positions (1st, 2nd, and 3rd), and COI was partitioned into two subsets (1st + 2nd and 3rd). In the phylogenetic analysis of mitogenomes, the concatenated alignment of 12 PCGs was partitioned by the three codon positions (Table S4). Node support was assessed with the ultrafast bootstrap approximation [18] with 10,000 replicates.

Bayesian ultrametric trees were reconstructed with BEAST 1.10 [19,20] with a relaxed lognormal clock and a birth–death tree prior. No calibrations were applied, and the ucld.mean parameter was set to 1.0. The substitution models were the same as in the ML analysis, and default priors were retained for the remaining parameters. The chain was run for 50 million generations, sampling every 25,000 generations, with a burn-in of 10%. Chain convergence was checked in Tracer v1.7 [21]; effective sample sizes (ESS) were above 200 for all parameters. The maximum clade credibility tree was generated in TreeAnnotator v1.10.4.

Relationships among haplotypes were illustrated using median-joining networks constructed in SplitsTree App 6.0.0 [22]. The network was reconstructed based on 60 specimens, each contributing a single sequence of at least 1113 bp. Sequences lacking a precise locality were excluded from the analysis, as were sequences from historical specimens, because they are substantially shorter.

sec.title: 2.3. Mitogenome Assembly and Annotation
sec.p: The quality of the raw reads was assessed with FastQC v0.12.1 [23]. Adapter sequences and low-quality bases were removed using Trimmomatic v0.41 (SLIDINGWINDOW: 4:20; MINLEN:36) [24], followed by a second quality assessment with FastQC. The nearly complete mitochondrial genomes were assembled using two independent de novo approaches. First, an assembly was performed with NOVOPlasty v3.4.5 [25] using a partial COI gene sequence of H. auritus (KX859285) as a seed.

In parallel, for some specimens the reads were assembled with MEGAHIT v1.2.9 [26,27]. MEGAHIT generated multiple contigs for each sample. We selected those matching the expected mitochondrial genome size for Hemiechinus (approximately 17,000–18,000 bp) and verified them by BLASTn searches against the NCBI nucleotide database (https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) (accessed on 1 November 2026). The results produced by both methods were consistent with each other. Raw reads for each specimen were then mapped onto their respective assembled sequences as references using BWA-MEM v0.7.17 [28].

Alignments were processed, and sequencing depth was calculated using SAMtools v1.17 [29]; the average coverage exceeded 40×, indicating sufficient read support for the reconstructed mitochondrial genomes. Coverage variation was observed mainly in the control region (D-loop), which contains short tandem repeats and represents a challenging region for assembly from short-read data. Therefore, the region was trimmed at the point where read depth dropped sharply to approximately 20×, as the assembly beyond this position was considered unreliable. Variant calling and consensus sequence generation were performed using BCFtools v1.17 [29].

The mitochondrial genome sequences obtained were annotated using the MITOS2 tool [30,31] on the Galaxy platform using default parameters. Their arrangement and orientation were then verified to be consistent with those of typical mammalian mitochondrial genomes. The 12 PCGs (excluding ND6) were extracted from the annotations and concatenated into a single alignment for each specimen. The concatenated PCGs were subsequently used for phylogenetic analyses and tree reconstruction. A full description of the mitogenomes obtained in our study is presented in Table S5.

sec.title: 2.4. Molecular Dating
sec.p: To mitigate potential bias caused by substitution rate decay in the cytb gene, we implemented a two-step dating procedure. First, we inferred a time-calibrated phylogeny for Erinaceinae in BEAST using an alignment of slowly evolving third-codon-position transversions (tv3) from 12 mitochondrial protein-coding genes. We applied secondary calibrations based on intergeneric divergence dates from Bannikova et al. [1], which allowed us to estimate the age and 95% highest posterior density (HPD) interval of the basal Hemiechinus node. In the second step, we estimated divergence times within H. auritus s. l. using the cytb alignment. This was accomplished by rescaling an uncalibrated cytb tree to the age of the basal Hemiechinus node estimated in the first step. The details of the procedure are given in Supplementary Materials SII: Molecular dating, text and Table S6.

sec.title: 2.5. Genetic Diversity and Demographic Parameters
sec.p: Genetic p-distances were computed using MEGA6 [32]. Genetic diversity indices (nucleotide and gene diversity for sample sets with N ≥ 10), mismatch distribution parameters (SSD for the sudden expansion model (SEM), raggedness index), the expansion parameter τ [33] together with its confidence interval (CI), as well as Tajima’s D [34] and Fu’s Fs [35] neutrality statistics, were determined in Arlequin 3.5 [36] on the basis of the cytb alignment. The significance of these statistics was assessed by producing 1000 random samples under the null hypothesis. An overall pattern of demographic history was characterized by means of the Bayesian Skyline Plot (BSP) approach [37], which permits estimation of changes in effective population size through time. Independent analyses were performed in BEAST v1.10.4 on several cytb alignments with N > 20 corresponding to separate haplogroups and population groups. A Bayesian skyline tree prior with ten groups and a strict clock model were applied. All other parameters were set as described above (see Section 2.2 Phylogenetic analysis). The resulting skyline plots were visualized in Tracer v1.7.2. To estimate the timing of expansions, the results were rescaled using the cytb substitution rate estimate obtained from the molecular dating analysis.

sec.title: 2.6. Biogeographic Paleo-Reconstructions
sec.p: Locality data were obtained from GBIF.org (GBIF Occurrence Download https://www.gbif.org/citation-guidelines (accessed on 21 April 2026), data set № 0037860-260409193756587) [38], the collections of ZMMU and ZIN (Zoological Institute, St. Petersburg, Russia), iNaturalist, the publications listed in Supplementary Materials SIII, and our field data (Tables S1-A and S7). This yielded 806 locality records spanning the species range (Figure S1); however, not all locations were genetically sampled to confirm the species identity and clade assignment.

We spatially filtered (thinned) the occurrence data prior to MaxEnt modelling. For each occurrence point, we calculated the distance to the nearest point and removed one point from each pair separated by less than 5 km. This spatial thinning partially mitigates spatial sampling bias. Because the thinned data were distributed relatively evenly across geographic space, we did not apply an additional sampling-bias correction. Background sampling was performed using the default MaxEnt settings (10,000 random points) within the study area (defined below) for each species or clade.

Species distribution models (SDMs) were based on climatic layers with a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds (ca. 1 km). Present-day bioclimatic variables (BioClim 1-19) were obtained from WorldClim version 2.1 [39]; paleoclimate data for the intervals 350–200 Kya were taken from the Oscillayers dataset [40].

The SDMs were built using the MaxEnt 3.4.0 software [41]. Data preparation for SDM with MaxEnt and operations with the resulting models were carried out using ArcGIS Pro 3.6: Copyright © 2025 Esri. The extent of the study area or of the “landscape of interest” significantly affects SDM results [42,43]. The study area was delimited by clipping the environmental layers to a rectangle that encompassed all occurrence points with a buffer of 4 degrees on each side. The present-day model was built using the default MaxEnt settings, which have been shown to be optimal for wide-ranging data [44]. The default MaxEnt settings include a regularization multiplier of 1, 10,000 background points, and automatic feature selection. The MaxEnt logistic output, which provides estimates of relative habitat suitability [43], was used. Most bioclimatic variables are correlated with one another, and including the full set may result in model overprediction. To prevent this, pairwise correlation coefficients among the 19 bioclimatic variables within the study area were computed with the “Band Collection Statistics” tool (Spatial Analyst Tools, standard ArcToolbox, ArcGIS Pro 3.6).

Based on this correlation matrix, the pairs of variables with the highest correlation coefficients were identified. For each such pair, two models were built (Table S8), each lacking one of the two variables, and their performance was compared using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC); the variable whose inclusion yielded the lower AUC was discarded. The procedure was repeated for successive pairs of strongly correlated variables until the exclusion of a variable caused a sharp drop in AUC.

Model performance and transferability were assessed by partitioning the data into training (75% of occurrence points) and testing (25%) subsets. SDM performance was evaluated on the testing subset using the standard evaluation metric provided in the MaxEnt output (corrected AUCROC). Spatially structured validation was not performed.

The present-day model built with the final reduced set of environmental variables was projected onto the paleoenvironmental datasets. Our analysis focused on scenarios of diversification among the main phylogeographic lineages. For each node, the time window to be examined was defined by the 95% HPD interval of its divergence time estimated by molecular dating. Within each window, we obtained models of relative habitat suitability (RHS) at 10-ky intervals. Among these models, we identified the earliest time slice showing a continuous distribution that was followed by several consecutive slices showing stable range fragmentation. We hypothesized that the onset of this fragmentation corresponds to the divergence at the respective node.

The continuous model output (values from 0 to 1) was converted into binary maps (0 or 1) delimiting the areas of actual species occurrence. For this conversion, we applied the “maximum training sensitivity plus specificity” threshold, which has been shown experimentally to give optimal results [45].

sec.title: 3.1. Cytb Data: Phylogenetic Trees, Network and Genetic Distances
sec.p: Phylogenetic analyses of the cytb dataset using maximum likelihood (ML) and BEAST (Figure 2 and Figures S2 and S3) recovered five highly supported main lineages, some of which are additionally structured at a finer scale. Their geographic distribution is presented in Figure 1. The level of divergence (p-distance) between the main lineages ranged from 2 to 4.23% (Table S9). The rationale for this structuring is provided below.

Northern phylogroup (N): southern Russia, the Crimean Peninsula, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, northern Turkmenistan, Western Siberia, Mongolian Dzungaria. This is the most widespread clade of H. auritus, exhibiting a relatively complex, albeit shallow, genetic structure (see also Figure 3 showing haplotype network). In the BEAST tree it is subdivided into North-western (NW) and North-central (NC) sublineages without reliable support, which differ by a p-distance of 1% and are recovered on the haplotype network (Figure 3). The NW and NC sublineages comprise specimens collected westwards and eastwards of the Lower Volga region, respectively. The former includes specimens from the North Caucasus, the Lower Volga region and Crimea. The latter is distributed in Central Asia, extending westwards to the Volga and eastwards to Mongolian Dzungaria. These sublineages are poorly supported, which may be partly explained by the unstable position of a smaller subclade comprising several specimens from the left bank of the Volga (A16-38, A22-02, A22-05). On the ML tree, this structure is less obvious.

Eastern phylogroup (E): most of Gobi, Alashan and adjacent deserts of south-eastern and central Mongolia and China. This is the most homogeneous clade, with haplotypes from the Govi Altai (Ömnögovi, south-central Mongolia) and Dornogovi (south-eastern Mongolia) occupying a basal position in the phylogroup.

South-western phylogroup (SW): the south-western part of the range. It includes four sublineages divergent by 0.7–1.5%: (1) north-eastern Africa (Egypt), (2) Cyprus and Israel, (3) the east bank of the Jordan River (Jordan) and the north-eastern edge of the Arabian Peninsula (Kuwait), (4) the south-central part of eastern Anatolia (Türkiye).
Transcaucasian (T): north of eastern Anatolia (Türkiye) and likely Armenia.

Southern phylogroup (S): Middle Asia (Afghanistan, Iran, Turkmenistan) and East Transcaucasia (Azerbaijan). The affiliation of the samples from Afghanistan with this clade was determined based on the analysis of COI sequences (Figure S4, see below). The position of H. collaris in the phylogenetic tree is unstable and receives low support in both the BEAST (Figure 2 and Figure S3) and ML (Figure S2) analyses; however, it is clearly associated with the Southern phylogroup. Thus, on present evidence, H. auritus mtDNA is not monophyletic with respect to H. collaris.

In general, haplotypes belonging to different phylogroups are distributed allopatrically; however, in one case, haplotypes of different lineages were found at the same locality (Figure 1). At a locality in south-western Mongolia (Govi-Altai, south-east of Lake Alag Nuur, loc. 49), adjacent to Mongolian Dzungaria, one of the three sampled hedgehogs carried a haplotype from the N phylogroup, whereas the other two carried haplotypes from the E phylogroup. Among Mongolian hedgehogs, a haplotype of the N clade was also found in Yolkhon (Mongolian Dzungaria, loc. 48).

sec.title: 3.2. Data from Concatenation of cytb and COI
sec.p: To examine in greater detail the evolutionary relationships among specimens from Turkmenistan, Iran, and Afghanistan we analyzed concatenated cytb and COI sequences using a limited dataset. The data on Afghan hedgehogs are restricted to two COI sequences from GenBank (MN326051 and MN326061). These sequences belong to specimens USNM:MAMM:602259 and USNM:MAMM:602256 from Kandahar, which is cited as the type locality for H. a. megalotis [46].

On the whole, the topology of the cytb + COI tree (Figure S4) corresponds to that of the cytb tree, demonstrating the same five main clades. We found that our specimens from the Kopetdag and Qazvin Province of Iran grouped with the Afghan hedgehogs, which indicates that the Southern lineage includes topotypical megalotis.

sec.title: 3.3. Mitogenomic Phylogenetic Tree
sec.p: Mitogenomic ML and Bayesian trees were reconstructed based on the dataset including representatives of each of the five cytb phylogroups (Figure 4). The phylogenetic analysis of the mitogenomic dataset recovered the same five distinctive lineages, albeit with higher support. The position of the S clade as the sister group to all other lineages was fully corroborated. Specimens of the N and E clades formed a well-supported group, whereas the specimen from the T clade (north-eastern Türkiye) was placed as the sister branch to the specimen of the SW clade (Egypt), albeit with moderate support in the ML analysis. The sister relationship between the N + E and SW + T groupings is highly supported.

sec.title: 3.4. Genetic Diversity and Demographic History
sec.p: The haplotype diversity was approximately the same in all tested groups, whereas nucleotide diversity was highest in the SW phylogroup and lowest in the E phylogroup. Both Fu’s Fs and Tajima’s D neutrality statistics were significantly negative for the N phylogroup (Table 1), thus indicating population growth in this part of the range. Mismatch distribution analysis showed a near-bell-shaped profile for the N sample (Figure 5A, Table S10). The skyline plot (Figure 6A) is consistent with demographic expansion peaking at ca. 12 Kya. We also performed neutrality tests and mismatch distribution analysis for the two subgroups of the N phylogroup (NW and NC). Tajima’s D and Fu’s Fs tests indicated demographic expansion in both the NW and NC samples (Table 1). However, a deviation from the bell-shaped mismatch distribution was detected in the NW sample (Figure 5E), whereas the bell-shaped mismatch distribution in the NC sample (Figure 5F) suggests a sudden population expansion in the past (Table S10). The skyline plot (Figure 6B) for the NC subgroup is also consistent with demographic expansion peaking at ~12.5 Kya.

A significant deviation from the null hypothesis of population stability was also found for the E sample, but only in Fu’s neutrality test. The skyline plot (Figure 6C) showed a smooth pattern of population growth with the highest rate at ca. 4 Kya. Mismatch distribution analysis showed a unimodal profile for the E sample and no deviation from the sudden-expansion model based on the SSD and raggedness index (Figure 5B).

In contrast, the S and SW phylogroups showed no deviation from the null hypothesis in Tajima’s and Fu’s Fs neutrality tests (Table 1) and a multimodal distribution in the mismatch distribution analysis (Figure 5C,D). The skyline plot for the SW clade shows no clear signal of expansion or decline (Figure 6D).

sec.title: 3.5. Divergence Times
sec.p: The divergence among lineages of H. auritus was estimated to have occurred during the late Middle and Late Pleistocene (Table 2). The radiation of subclades within the N clade represents the most recent diversification event in the species.

sec.title: 3.6. Biogeographic Paleo-Range Reconstructions
sec.p: We modelled potential past distributions and produced hypothetical diversification scenarios for all Pleistocene nodes. The nodes corresponding to the sequence of major divergence events are numbered in Figure 2.

sec.title: 3.6.1. Node 1—Divergence of the S Clade
sec.p: The model was based on occurrence records of H. auritus and H. collaris. Reconstructions of potential paleo-ranges using SDM revealed that a common ancestor of H. auritus s. l. with a continuous distribution across the area of the current range could have existed during the warm and wet climate of the interglacial stage of the 330 Kya glacial cycle (Figure 7A). According to the model, under the cold and dry climate of the glacial maximum at 250 Kya, the range may have contracted and become fragmented into two potential isolates: a south-eastern one, probably corresponding to the S clade, and a north-western one, probably corresponding to the remaining populations of H. auritus (Figure 7B).

sec.title: 3.6.2. Node 2—Subdivision of the Northern + Eastern and South-Western Clades of H. auritus
sec.p: The model was based on occurrence records of H. auritus. During the thermal and precipitation maxima of the interglacial stage of the glacial cycle at 200 Kya, the potential geographic range of H. auritus was reconstructed as continuous across an area largely coinciding with the current range of the species, although less extensive eastward in Mongolia and China than at present (Figure 7C). According to the model, the range was constricted and fragmented into two isolates, a northern one (the N clade) and a south-western one (the SW + T clade), at the beginning of the cold and dry climate of the glaciation phase at 180 Kya (Figure 7D).

sec.title: 3.6.3. Node 3—Subdivision of the South-Western Range of H. auritus into the SW and T Clades
sec.p: The model was based on occurrence records of hedgehogs of the SW and T clades. According to the model, as the glaciation phase continued at 180–150 Kya, the south-western part of the potential range of H. auritus may have contracted at 180 Kya (Figure S5A) and become fragmented at 170 Kya into two potential isolates: a south-western one, probably corresponding to the SW clade and less extensive westward in Egypt and Libya than at present, and a small northern one, probably corresponding to the T clade (Figure S5B). During the thermal and precipitation maxima of the interglacial stage of the glacial cycle at 120 Kya (Figure 8A), the range of the SW clade was subdivided into three fragments, western, central and eastern. At the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), the eastern fragment disappeared (Figure 8B).

sec.title: 3.6.4. Node 4—Subdivision of the Northern Clades of H. auritus into the N and E Clades
sec.p: The model was based on occurrence records of hedgehogs of the N and E clades. The potential geographic range of the northern fragment of H. auritus was continuous across an area coinciding with the current range of the species during the thermal and precipitation maxima of the interglacial stage of the glacial cycle at 120 Kya (Figure 9A). At the beginning of the glacial phase, this part of the range began to constrict and fragment into several isolates: two western and six eastern at 110 Kya (Figure 9B), four western and eight eastern at 70 Kya (Figure 9C) and finally one western (in the northern Caspian lowlands, the Kyzylkum and northern Karakum Deserts) and one eastern (in the foothills of the Eastern Tianshan) at the LGM (Figure 9D).

sec.title: 3.7. Paleorange of the S Clade
sec.p: At the same time, the potential distribution of the S clade, as estimated from environmental suitability, was continuous across an area coinciding with the current range of the species (although significantly less extensive westward than at present) during the thermal and precipitation maxima of the interglacial stage of the glacial cycle at 200 Kya (Figure 10A). The reconstruction for the onset of the cold and dry glacial phase at 180 Kya suggests that the range may have contracted and become fragmented into two potential isolates: a south-western one, probably corresponding to the S clade, and an eastern one, probably corresponding to H. collaris (Figure 10B). At this time, the potential range of the S clade appears to have extended considerably westward and north-westward into Iran and south-western Turkmenistan. During the thermal and precipitation maxima of the interglacial stage of the glacial cycle at 120 Kya (Figure 10C) the range of the S clade expanded further northward into southern Turkmenistan and eastern Transcaucasia. At the LGM, the modelled range was constricted and fragmented into four isolates (Figure 10D).

sec.title: 4.1. Phylogeographic Structure and Phylogeographic Gaps
sec.p: The evolutionary success of the long-eared hedgehog is reflected in its vast range—the largest in the entire family Erinaceidae—and, as is now evident, in a remarkable phylogeographic structure, which is more differentiated than reported in previous studies [1,12]. H. auritus was recovered as a complex of five deeply divergent, reciprocally monophyletic lineages, three of which are, in turn, structured at a finer scale. The two phylogroups distributed in the northern part of the range (N and E) form a clade, whereas the phylogroups endemic to the southern part of the range (S, SW, and T) appear as a paraphyletic assemblage.

The E phylogroup, which consists mainly of Mongolian samples, is particularly distinctive. The distinctness of the Mongolian population relative to those of Kazakhstan and western Central Asia is not unique to long-eared hedgehogs; a similar phylogeographic pattern, whether within a single species or between closely related species, has been observed in these regions for Phodopus campbelli/Phodopus sungorus [47], phylogroups of Ellobius tancrei [48], and the species complex Meriones meridianus [49].

Our data also reveal several potential contact zones and barriers between genetic lineages. The first is the area where the N and E clades co-occur, in the Alag Nuur Lake depression in south-western Mongolia. This area is directly adjacent to Mongolian Dzungaria, where an N-clade haplotype was found (Yolkhon), suggesting that Dzungaria is inhabited by the western N lineage, a pattern also observed in other desert mammals, such as Meriones ex gr. meridianus [49] and Dipus sagitta s. l. [50].

Second, our data tentatively suggest that the Amu Darya River separates the N and S clades along its upper and middle reaches. The S clade is common on the left (western) bank, while the N clade inhabits the right (eastern) bank. However, in the lower reaches of the river, a hedgehog from the left bank (loc. 18: Tashauz) carried an N-clade haplotype, suggesting that the river is not a complete barrier in its lower course.

Third, the N clade shows an east–west subdivision in the Lower Volga valley, suggesting that the river may act as a barrier between western and eastern populations of hedgehogs. Although the haplogroups on the left and right banks of the Volga lack statistical support, a similar east–west dichotomy has been reported for other small mammals in this region, including Spermophilus pygmaeus [51], Ellobius talpinus [52], and Nothocricetulus migratorius [53]. These examples suggest that the Volga is an important barrier separating sibling species, subspecies or populations of steppe and semidesert mammals.

sec.title: 4.2. Potential Scenario of Diversification and Historical Range Dynamics
sec.p: Our phylogenetic reconstruction suggests that H. auritus s. l. originated in south-western Asia: the southern lineages (S, SW and T) form a paraphyletic assemblage with the S clade at the base of the tree, whereas the two northern lineages (N and E) occupy a derived position as sister clades. The pronounced phylogeographic subdivision of the S and SW lineages suggests a long evolutionary history, during which these lineages persisted as multiple populations. Neither the neutrality tests, the mismatch distributions (multimodal profiles), nor the skyline plot for the SW clade revealed a statistically detectable signal of population expansion in these lineages. In contrast, the E phylogroup and the subclades of the N phylogroup lack pronounced structure across their extensive ranges, and the neutrality tests and demographic analyses (S-shaped skylines and unimodal mismatch distributions) reveal stronger signatures consistent with rapid, likely postglacial expansion and relatively recent colonization of the eastern and northern parts of the range. All these demographic inferences should nevertheless be interpreted with caution, as they are based on a single maternally inherited locus, and it is currently difficult to distinguish spatial from demographic expansion and to partial out the effects of population structure and sampling heterogeneity [54].

The hypothesis of a south-western Asian origin is further supported by the paleo-reconstructions, which indicate that at ~250 Kya (the time of separation of the S lineage) the potential range included large areas in the Middle East, north-eastern Africa, South Asia, and Iran, but only a few parts of Central Asia. It should be noted that the absence of spatially structured validation in cases where the study area is large and the distribution of occurrence records is heterogeneous limits confidence in model robustness and transferability, particularly for nodes 1 and 2. Also, one should acknowledge that the uncertainty in the initial lineage assignments may have propagated into the lineage-specific SDMs. The reconstructed paleodistributions should therefore be regarded as biologically plausible scenarios consistent with the genetic data, rather than definitive reconstructions of past ranges.

In the two northern lineages, range contraction and fragmentation coincided with cold stages: both the N and E lineages had continuous distributions during the Last Interglacial, whereas their ranges were substantially reduced and fragmented during the LGM. This agrees with the demographic signals of recent, likely postglacial expansion in these lineages. Our results are thus consistent with the view that glacial maxima promoted range fragmentation in desert and steppe mammals, despite the simultaneous expansion of arid open landscapes, and that this fragmentation was followed by postglacial recolonization, as reported in several recent studies [55,56]. Nevertheless, alternative phylogeographic patterns have been suggested for other small mammal taxa [57]. The extent to which this discrepancy reflects interspecific variation in responses to identical climatic shifts, rather than inconsistencies in molecular clock estimates, warrants further investigation.

sec.title: 4.3. Genetic Lineages and Morphological Subspecies
sec.p: Comparison between mitochondrial lineages and morphological subspecies is hampered by the lack of a universally accepted subspecies taxonomy. In the most recent edition of Mammal Species of the World (MSW3), five subspecies are listed: auritus, albulus, aegyptius, libycus, and megalotis [6]. More recently, however, Best [3] reduced this number to three: auritus, albulus, and megalotis. Here, we primarily follow the comprehensive revision of intraspecific morphological variation and taxonomy of the long-eared hedgehog by Zaitsev [7]. He recognized six subspecies: H. a. auritus (northern parts of the species range), H. a. aegyptius (south-western parts of the species range), H. a. persicus (southern Turkmenistan and adjacent parts of Iran), H. a. minor (south-west Siberia), H. a. megalotis (Afghanistan, Balochistan), and H. a. collaris (India, Pakistan), thereby subsuming H. collaris into H. auritus. As a modification of this system, we also consider H. a. albulus (eastern part of the range), following Corbet [2], and H. a. calligoni (Transcaucasia and potentially some parts of the Middle East), following Harrison and Bates [58].

Our data indicate, consistent with Özmen et al. [12], that the phylogeographic structure of the long-eared hedgehog is partly congruent with the principal morphological subspecies. The N clade corresponds to H. a. auritus Gmelin, 1770, whose type locality (Astrakhan) lies within the range of this clade. However, it also includes a specimen from Altai, where Zaitsev recognized a distinct subspecies, H. a. minor [7], as well as specimens from Ciscaucasia, which, according to Niethammer [8] and Zaitsev [7], should be inhabited by H. a. aegyptius. The available name for the E clade could be H. a. albulus Stoliczka, 1872. For now, however, this remains merely a supposition, since the type locality of H. a. albulus is in south-western Xinjiang (Sanju, Yarkand), an area that remains unstudied. At the same time, Zaitsev [7] and Corbet [2] suggested that albulus is distributed in south-eastern Kazakhstan, which does not agree with the mtDNA pattern, because only the N haplogroup was found in Kazakhstan. The assumption that H. a. albulus occurs in Kazakhstan is probably the reason why Zaitsev included it in the nominotypical subspecies, as he did not examine Mongolian or Chinese specimens [7].

The SW clade likely corresponds to H. a. aegyptius Fischer, 1829, whose type locality is in Egypt. However, the range of this clade is smaller than that of the subspecies as treated by Niethammer [8] or Zaitsev [7], as it does not include Ciscaucasia or Transcaucasia.

The known range of the Transcaucasian lineage includes the type locality of H. a. calligoni Satunin, 1901 (the foothills of Mount Ararat) [12]. Most authors [6,7] have synonymized calligoni with aegyptius, while others [58] consider it distinct and suggest that it is distributed in eastern and southern Anatolia, the Levant, and Mesopotamia. This view is not supported by the mitochondrial data: the T lineage is probably restricted to north-eastern Anatolia and parts of Transcaucasia, whereas the areas further south belong to the range of the SW lineage. Additional sampling is needed to establish the limits of the T lineage.

The S clade most likely corresponds to H. a. megalotis; however, this is the most complex case, as the taxonomic status of the megalotis form has itself been repeatedly debated. Originally described from Kandahar as H. megalotis Blyth, 1845, and formerly regarded as a distinct species, its species status was later questioned by Niethammer [8] who suggested that it intergrades with more northern forms. While some researchers continued to treat megalotis as a species [10,46,58,59], others supported Niethammer’s treatment [2,6,7], which is the prevailing view at present. Although megalotis is now unanimously recognized as a valid taxon, its content and distribution remain unclear (i.e., how far westwards it extends in Iran and whether it includes the populations of southern Turkmenistan). For example, Zaitsev considered H. a. megalotis proper to be restricted to Balochistan and Afghanistan, and recognized the populations of southern Turkmenistan (Kopetdag) and parts of Iran as a related but distinct subspecies, H. a. persicus (syn. chorassanicus) [7]. The existence in southern Turkmenistan of a subspecies separate from H. a. auritus and H. a. megalotis was also acknowledged by other authors [8,60].

The range of the S mitochondrial lineage is much wider than the range of megalotis, regardless of the taxonomic treatment. It includes not only Afghanistan and southern Turkmenistan but also most of the Karakum Desert and eastern Transcaucasia—areas that were never considered part of the H. a. megalotis range. The S lineage is also found in northern Iran and is likely to occur in the eastern and southern parts of the country; however, the details of its phylogeography on the Iranian Plateau remain poorly known.

Regarding the other genetic lineages, the subspecies status and origin of the Cypriot population have been in dispute. The name dorotheae [61] was initially applied to hedgehogs from Cyprus, and it was previously assumed that long-eared hedgehogs were introduced to Cyprus by humans [62]. In our phylogeny, haplotypes from Cyprus and Israel formed a joint subclade within the South-western clade and this grouping was recovered as sister to the Egyptian subclade. This similarity between Cypriot, Israeli and Egyptian haplotypes supports an origin of this subclade in North Africa or the Levant rather than Anatolia.

The distribution of the five mitochondrial phylogroups (based on our data) and their potentially corresponding morphological subspecies (inferred from the analysis of literature, GBIF.org, iNaturalist, museum collections, and our data) is shown in Figure S1. Note that non-genotyped localities were assigned to genetic lineages a priori; these assignments are therefore provisional.

Although mitochondrial data alone are insufficient for a taxonomic revision of species complexes such as H. auritus s. l., they provide a foundation for hypotheses that can be tested by future genomic studies. First, the genetic divergence between the lineages corresponding to H. a. auritus and H. a. megalotis (p-distance 3.84%) as well as between auritus and aegyptius (3.31%) or calligoni and megalotis (4.23%) falls within the range reported both for closely related species and for highly divergent subspecies (2–11%) [63]. These lineages might therefore tentatively be regarded as species in statu nascendi; however, their true taxonomic status can only be determined by assessing gene flow across their contact zones, which are probably located in Transcaucasia, western Iran, eastern Türkiye, and northern Turkmenistan.

Second, the taxonomic status of H. collaris, which appears to be closely related to H. a. megalotis, requires further scrutiny, as it is represented in our dataset by a single specimen (ZIN6328), whose position in the phylogenetic trees is poorly supported. Furthermore, the morphological identification of this specimen is incomplete because the skull has been lost, although its external dimensions (hindfoot length of ca. 33 mm) and spine coloration correspond to H. collaris. The locality of this specimen (between Hyderabad and Rohri) falls within the species range reported in the literature [5,59], but lies at its western boundary. Moreover, H. a. megalotis also occurs in Pakistan, where it is restricted to western regions (mainly Balochistan), whereas H. collaris has been recorded in the Indus Valley [59]. Thus, the proximity of the range boundaries of H. a. megalotis and H. collaris increases both the risk of misidentification and the possibility of mitochondrial introgression in a potential contact zone.

sec.title: 4.4. Conservation Implications
sec.p: The present phylogeographic results for H. auritus identify geographic components of evolutionary diversity that may deserve particular attention in future conservation assessments. The long-eared hedgehog is globally classified as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List [3]. However, the geographically structured and deeply divergent mitochondrial lineages identified within the species represent an important component of intraspecific evolutionary diversity that could be overlooked if the species is treated as a single homogeneous unit. Lineages with restricted ranges (the Transcaucasian lineage and the population of Cyprus) deserve special attention.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: In conclusion, our data suggest that H. auritus comprises several divergent lineages, some of which may represent early stages of speciation. However, the evolutionary history of the long-eared hedgehog proposed here should be interpreted with caution, given the limitations of relying on a single maternally inherited locus, the provisional assignment of non-genotyped populations to genetic lineages, and the assumptions inherent in SDM reconstructions. Determining the taxonomic rank of the phylogroups within H. auritus will require a careful analysis of multilocus nuclear data. Furthermore, morphological variation within the genus Hemiechinus is considerable, and several morphologically distinct taxa (e.g., Hemiechinus microtis Laptev, 1925 from Uzbekistan) remain genetically unstudied. Future studies should also aim to identify contact zones between the phylogroups precisely and to determine whether, and to what extent, gene flow among them is restricted.
